question:
Based on the chest X-ray figures, which feature most strongly supports the diagnosis of malignant pleural mesothelioma in this patient?
A) Bilateral pleural effusion
B) Thick nodular pleural mass impinging on mediastinal structures
C) Bilateral lung volume reduction
D) Large central pulmonary mass
E) Diffuse interstitial lung disease
F) Osteolytic lesion of the sternum

observations.value: thick, irregular, nodular pleural soft-tissue mass encasing the left lung and abutting/impinging on mediastinal structures (aorta, pulmonary artery, heart) in Figures 1 and 3; right pleura also thickened but less prominently in Figure 2
minimal or no free fluid visible; opacities are predominantly solid/mass-like rather than dependent fluid
left lung volume reduced due to encasement and atelectasis; right lung appears near-normal volume

hypotheses.name: malignant pleural mesothelioma
hypotheses.basis: Diffuse, nodular, circumferential pleural thickening with mediastinal invasion and contralateral pleural involvement is highly characteristic of epithelioid or biphasic mesothelioma; absence of discrete lung mass favors pleural primary over metastatic carcinoma

hypotheses.name: metastatic pleural disease (e.g., from lung or breast cancer)
hypotheses.basis: Nodular pleural thickening can occur in metastases; however, the diffuse, rind-like encasement and bilateral involvement are more typical of mesothelioma; requires histopathology for distinction

hypotheses.name: pleural infection (e.g., tuberculous empyema with fibrosis)
hypotheses.basis: Can cause pleural thickening, but typically less nodular and less aggressive mediastinal impingement; no associated cavitation or lymphadenopathy seen here

discriminators.question: Which option describes the dominant pleural finding that distinguishes mesothelioma from other causes?
Is the pleural abnormality bilateral and primarily solid (mass) rather than fluid?
Is the opacity extrapulmonary (pleural) versus intrapulmonary (central mass)?

hypotheses.name: Malignant pleural mesothelioma (epithelioid or biphasic subtype)
hypotheses.basis: The combination of unilateral, nodular, circumferential pleural thickening with mediastinal impingement and diaphragmatic extension is highly characteristic of malignant pleural mesothelioma, especially in the absence of other primary malignancy or asbestos exposure history (not provided). This pattern distinguishes it from metastatic pleural disease (often nodular but less circumferential) or benign fibrous tumor (typically localized).
